title: Yankee Stadium cooling tower tests positive for Legionella bacteria
content:
One of 10 South Bronx cooling towers that has tested positive for Legionella bacteria is located at Yankee Stadium, officials with the New York City Health Department announced Sunday. Each of the towers has been ordered to be cleaned and disinfected by Sept. 14, as an investigation continues into the borough’s recent outbreak of Legionnaires’ disease.

“To reduce the risk of ongoing exposure while culture testing continues, the Health Department is requiring cooling towers with a positive PCR (polymerase chain reaction) result to conduct a full remediation, including draining, cleaning, and disinfection,” health officials said in a news release.

The department said it’s unknown whether any of the towers that tested positive contributed to the outbreak. PCR tests can detect Legionella bacteria DNA but cannot determine whether the bacteria are alive or dead, according to the news release, and only live bacteria can cause the illness.

It was not immediately known where the tower — which is situated at 1 E. 161st St., the same address as Yankee Stadium — was specifically located. On Sunday, the New York Yankees hosted the New York Mets, concluding a six-game homestand that began last Tuesday. Health officials launched an investigation Thursday after identifying a cluster of Legionnaires’ disease cases in the South Bronx.

The Yankees did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“Anyone who lives, works, or has visited the area since late August and develops flu-like symptoms should contact a health care provider immediately,” the release cautioned.

The CDC defines Legionnaires’ disease “as a type of serious pneumonia caused by a type of bacteria called Legionella.” Its symptoms typically develop within two to 14 days of exposure to the bacteria, with ailments similar to those of pneumonia, including coughing and shortness of breath.

Most cases can be treated successfully.

Cooling towers, which release mist into the air, have been linked to past outbreaks of Legionnaires’ disease, according to health officials.

Sunday’s news follows a recent outbreak in the borough that has killed one person and infected nine others. The outbreak comes after a separate incident over the summer in the Upper East Side of Manhattan. That outbreak, which was declared over in July, claimed the lives of 11 people, with more than 90 experiencing infection.
